prime.problem: A neuron can stop learning with no error or warning. Nothing crashes and the loss still goes down, but some units never change again, so the net quietly trains with fewer neurons than you paid for.
prime.fits: The saturated-tanh card showed tanh units stuck at ±1 in your MLP. This card asks the same question of every common nonlinearity, using the local-gradient idea from micrograd's tanh backward.
expect: dead neuron = flat for every example
dying ReLU from a too-big step
prime.goal: Predict, from a nonlinearity's shape, where it blocks gradients and whether its units can die, and check it by computing each local gradient with autograd.

attend: Why does a flat stretch of the curve stop the weights before it from learning, not just the output after it?
What turns an ordinary "off for this example" ReLU unit into a dead one?
Sigmoid has the smallest flat share of the three. Why does it still starve deep nets of gradient?
In the shock experiment, when do the units actually die: in the huge step, or afterwards?
What does Leaky ReLU's 0.01 slope buy, and what does it fail to fix?

must: Backward multiplies h.grad by the local gradient f′(hpreact) → on a flat part f′ ≈ 0 → hpreact.grad ≈ 0 → W1 and b1 for that unit get ≈ 0 gradient → the unit stops learning

ReLU's slope is exactly 0 for x ≤ 0 → a unit whose preactivation is ≤ 0 on every example gets exactly 0 gradient → its weights never move → it stays dead (a bad init or one oversized lr step can put it there)
tanh/sigmoid saturate in both tails, and sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25 → gradients shrink at every layer even when nothing is saturated → the damage compounds with depth
Leaky ReLU gives negative inputs slope 0.01 instead of 0 → no input is fully flat → units can't die, but a unit stuck below zero learns at only 1% speed
elevated: Dead is judged over all training examples, not one batch → about half of a healthy ReLU layer is off for any single input, and that is fine → check dead units with (preact <= 0).all(0) over the whole set, not one batch's histogram
reference: the formulas: tanh′ = 1 − t², σ′ = σ(1 − σ), ReLU′ = 1[x > 0], Leaky′ = 1 or 0.01

compress.prompt: From memory, draw one hidden neuron (hpreact → f → h) and the backward arrow through it. Mark where the local gradient multiplies in, then explain in 3–5 sentences what makes a neuron dead and why ReLU is the one that can die for good.
checklist: the gradient reaching W1 is multiplied by f′(hpreact)
flat part → f′ ≈ 0 → no learning signal for that unit's weights
dead = flat for every training example, not just some
ReLU is exactly 0 for x ≤ 0, so an all-negative unit gets exactly 0 gradient
causes: bad init or one too-large update; Leaky ReLU's 0.01 slope prevents death

retrieve.q: Explain why a unit that sits on a flat part of its nonlinearity stops its own incoming weights from learning, even when the loss gradient above it is large.
answer: chain rule: hpreact.grad = f′(hpreact) * h.grad
f′ ≈ 0 zeroes the product however big h.grad is
W1 and b1 get their gradient only through hpreact.grad

retrieve.q: Walk through the lab's shock experiment with lr 100: what happens in the shock step, in the next few steps, and over the following 1000 steps, and why do the dead units never come back?
answer: the shock step itself kills no units (scratch rerun)
it throws the net off, so the next steps see huge losses (38,537 two steps later) and huge gradients
those gradients push many units' preactivations ≤ 0 on all data: 41 dead by the third step, 188/200 at the end
a dead unit's local gradient is exactly 0, so its W1 column gets 0 gradient and stays put

retrieve.q: You are choosing a hidden nonlinearity for a deep net. Compare tanh, sigmoid, ReLU and Leaky ReLU on how each can starve the gradient. When is plain ReLU still a fine choice?
answer: tanh: flat tails past |x| ≈ 3 (40.1% of [−5, 5])
sigmoid: few flat regions (8.3%), but slope ≤ 0.25 shrinks every layer at least 4×
ReLU: slope 1 when on, but exactly 0 when off, so units can die (50.0% flat)
Leaky: never flat, but stuck units learn at 1%
ReLU is fine with good init, normalisation and a sane lr: 0/200 dead at lr 0.1 in the lab

retrieve.q: In the lab, 25 of 200 Leaky ReLU units ended up all-negative after the lr-30 shock. Why aren't they counted as dead, and why is their loss still better than ReLU's?
answer: their local gradient is 0.01, not 0, so some gradient still reaches their weights
they still pass a small signal forward (0.01x), so they aren't pure zeros
measured loss: 2.4754 vs 2.5262 for ReLU at the same shock

compare.q: That card finds tanh units stuck at ±1; this one finds ReLU units stuck at 0. What is the same failure underneath, and how does each one's escape route differ?
answer: same: the local gradient is ≈ 0, so the incoming weights stop learning
tanh: f′ = 1 − t² is tiny but never exactly 0, so a unit can drift back if its inputs change
ReLU: f′ is exactly 0, so an all-negative unit gets exactly 0 gradient
both are prevented upstream by keeping preactivations small (W1 × 0.2, or Kaiming)

compare.q: Kaiming init uses gain √2 for ReLU and 5/3 for tanh. How does each gain follow from the curve shapes on this card, and which death cause (init or lr) does it address?
answer: ReLU zeroes half of its inputs, so √2 restores the lost variance
tanh squashes its input, so 5/3 pushes back against the squeeze
the scale keeps preactivations near the steep part at init
it fixes the init cause, not the too-big-lr cause

predict.q: A dead ReLU unit's W1 column gets exactly zero gradient. But the embedding table C keeps training through the other units. Can a dead unit ever come back to life? Commit to yes or no, and to rarely or often.
predict.answer: Yes, but rarely. The dead test uses C[Xtr] @ W1 + b1, and C keeps moving, so a dead unit's inputs can drift until one example lands above zero. In a scratch rerun of the lab's lr-30 shock, the dead count went 23 → 38 → 44 → 42 → 53 over 5000 more steps at lr 0.1. It fell once (44 → 42), so a couple of units revived, but more kept dying than came back.

apply.task: Copy labs/dead-neurons.py into your scratch folder and add a ReLU run with shock lr 50. Before running, predict where it falls between the lr-30 result (23/200 dead) and the lr-100 result (188/200). Then, after the 1000 recovery steps, mark the dead units, save a copy of W1, train 100 more steps at lr 0.1, and print the largest absolute change in any dead unit's W1 column.
apply.done: You see 87/200 dead at shock lr 50, and the largest change in a dead unit's W1 column over those 100 steps is exactly 0.0.
apply.hint: Get the dead mask with (C[Xtr].view(-1, 30) @ W1 + b1 <= 0).all(0) under torch.no_grad(), save w0 = W1.detach().clone(), and after the extra steps take (W1 - w0).abs().sum(0)[mask].max().

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the flat-share ranking, or whether a dead unit can come back?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why sigmoid hurts deep nets despite a small flat share?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: big lr step → huge gradients, or huge gradients → all-negative preactivations?
Where in your own MLP would you look first for dead units, and with what one-line check?
What will you carry into the Kaiming-init card?
